articles.title: 'The biggest loser' in Washington: Nobel Prize-winning economist says Scott Bessent won't get interest rates down
articles.summary: He also compared Bessent to another fiery speaker, Iraq’s “Baghdad Bob.”
articles.body:
Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent isn't known for holding back at the podium. His remarks have made headlines, and some economists seem to have had enough.

Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman argued (1) on Substack that Bessent's recent comments evoke another fiery speaker, former Iraqi Minister of Foreign Affairs Muhammad Saeed Al-Sahhaf — known more prominently in the West as "Baghdad Bob."

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

A record 45% of central banks plan to grow gold reserves — and many investors are following suit. Get your free gold IRA guide from Priority Gold

Krugman pointed to Bessent's declaration on Sept. 8 that "I am the house now" (2) while daring investors to bet against him.

Bessent seemingly backed up this statement by attempting to lower borrowing costs through buying back $6 billion in government debt (3) to reduce U.S. Treasury yields. However, by early October, both 10- and 30-year yields actually rose to their highest levels since 2002 (4).

That's the opposite of what was meant to happen.

These events led Krugman to call Bessent the "Baghdad Bob of bonds," arguing that the once well-respected Bessent is the "biggest loser" in the White House who has greatly damaged his credibility.

Krugman isn't alone in this critique either. A recent Bloomberg article (5) suggests that Bessent "risks boxing himself in with his prognostications on gasoline prices, the housing market and the economy."

Regardless of Bessent's potential missteps, these events highlight the strong forces driving the $30 trillion-plus U.S. Treasury market (6) — and that even the secretary of the Treasury is struggling to combat them.

Bond yields can rise because of factors such as inflation fears, high issuance of bonds, low demand for bonds and the potential for higher policy interest rates from the Federal Reserve.

Contributing factors to current bond yields include a strong U.S. economy (7) and high oil prices, heavy bond issuance (8) by tech firms raising money to fund AI, and a five-year U.S. Treasury note auction in September that went poorly (9) (and may signal weak demand for U.S. Treasuries).

articles.title: CIA officer admits to creating fake top secret government program to steal over $190M, including gold bars | TechCrunch
articles.summary: CIA officer David Rush, who worked on highly sensitive intelligence programs, reached a plea deal with U.S. prosecutors after he was caught siphoning money and gold with a fake government contract.
articles.body:
A now-former officer with the Central Intelligence Agency has pleaded guilty to stealing almost $200 million, including hundreds of gold bars, as part of a fraudulent scheme masquerading as a top secret government program.

The U.S. Department of Justice on Tuesday confirmed that David J. Rush, a Virginia resident, admitted to one count of wire fraud linked to running the fabricated operation and defrauding the government while he was a CIA officer. In a statement, prosecutors said that Rush lied about his education and military experience to gain a position at the CIA, and used his access as an employee to set up the top secret and highly compartmentalized program with the intention of using it to funnel U.S. government funds into his possession.

During his arrest, law enforcement found more than $46 million worth of gold bars in Rush’s house linked to the long-running fraud scheme, along with cars, watches, and over $2 million in cash.

The plea deal means that Rush escapes trial, as much as the U.S. government likely avoids having to explain in open court how Rush evaded vetting scrutiny to join the U.S. intelligence agency, and how actions went undetected for more than a year.

Rush was until recently a senior CIA officer who, according to earlier reports , worked for a division of the CIA since 2010 that develops hacking tools and techniques for carrying out espionage. Per court filings , Rush had significant authority over government intelligence programs and spending.

Over the course of 2025, Rush used his position to fabricate a so-called special access program, which are surveillance or intelligence-gathering operations so sensitive that only a few people are read into them. Special access programs, or SAPs, require special clearance that not even the most cleared individuals in government are granted access to. According to The Washington Post , Rush constructed the compartmentalized program under the guise of a fake “continuity of government” plan, aimed at keeping the government functioning in the event of a war, natural disaster, or some other destructive catastrophe. As part of the scheme, Rush used the program and fake government contract to trick an unnamed defense contractor into buying large amounts of gold that Rush then pocketed.

According to The Post, the case astounded officials as Rush’s duties at the CIA involved work with one of the government’s “most sensitive intelligence-gathering programs,” with details so sensitive that only a few senior U.S. intelligence officials and lawmakers know of its existence. The Post withheld details of that program from publication as its disclosure could “jeopardize ongoing intelligence-gathering operations.”

Court filings said that by virtue of his position, Rush “effectively acted as his own approving official, enabling him to expend substantial amounts of United States government money without meaningful scrutiny.”

Rush is scheduled to be sentenced in late January 2027 and faces up to 20 years in prison.

articles.title: Watch live: Hegseth delivers remarks as USS Abraham Lincoln returns
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will welcome home sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln Wednesday afternoon in San Diego, following the aircraft carrier’s extended deployment to the Middle East. Hegseth is set to address the crew as the aircraft carrier returns to the U.S. after more than 280 days without a port call, including military operations…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will welcome home sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln Wednesday afternoon in San Diego, following the aircraft carrier’s extended deployment to the Middle East.

Hegseth is set to address the crew as the aircraft carrier returns to the U.S. after more than 280 days without a port call, including military operations against Iran.

The lengthy term drew scrutiny from lawmakers over reports of food and supply shortages , poor living conditions and sailors’ deteriorating mental health. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao also recently told Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) that eight sailors assigned to the carrier strike group attempted suicide during the deployment.

Hegseth and President Trump have defended conditions aboard the ship, arguing that the reports “completely misrepresented” the situation.

The Pentagon chief’s remarks are scheduled to begin at 2:10 p.m. EDT.

articles.title: What The Social Reckoning gets right — and wrong
articles.summary: Aaron Sorkin’s “Social Reckoning” film is based on the true story of Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen’s leaks to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz.
articles.body: Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoning has its fair share of cinematic flair, but many details in the story hew closely to real life. The movie tells the story of how Frances Haugen, a Facebook civic integrity product manager, came to leak a large trove of internal documents to Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz, in what would later become a 2021 series called “The Facebook Files.” In both real life and in the film, Haugen’s leaks lead her to testify as a congressional whistleblower. The final frames of the movie describe the impact she had even after that closing scene, speaking before governments around the world and bolstering lawsuits against Meta nationwide with the internal communications she disclosed. The film’s Haugen, played by Mikey Madison, says that she really believes in Facebook, echoing a message the real Haugen left for her colleagues just before she signed off for her last day in May 2021. “I don’t hate Facebook,” she wrote on the company’s internal message board, according to The Journal. “I love Facebook. I want to save it.” Sorkin, both directing and screenwriting the semi-follow up to 2010’s The Social Network, which he only wrote, took some liberties with the dialogue and the chronology of the movie. The most obvious is that he condensed the timeline and shifted major events forward by several months. Some key moments in the film — Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) preparing for a congressional hearing about misinformation and extremism and Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) getting ready to publish the first Facebook Files report — occur on the same day, which happens to be January 6th, 2021, amid the insurrection at the US Capitol. In reality, Zuckerberg testified in the House alongside other tech CEOs in March 2021, and the first installment of the Facebook Files wasn’t published until that September. But the movie pulls directly from Horwitz’ investigation and the documents that Haugen collected, which showed how the company applied its content moderation policies in inconsistent ways, drove users toward hate groups, and had meager responses to apparent human trafficking on the platform. Meta declined to provide a comment on the movie, but in past statements, the company has referred to the documents collected by Haugen and their recounting in the Facebook Files as cherry-picked to serve a specific narrative. Zuckerberg called the reporting Facebook Files “a coordinated effort to selectively use leaked documents to paint a false picture of our company” during a 2021 earnings call after the initial reports were released, and said that when faced with “impossible tradeoffs … these questions are not primarily about our business, but about balancing different difficult social values.” Here’s what you should know about the real life events underpinning the film. Losing a friend to the misinformation rabbit hole inspired Haugen The Social Reckoning opens with a young blonde woman standing next to her overheating car on the side of a highway. When cops pull up to ask if she’s okay and smell alcohol on her breath, the exchange quickly grows tense. The woman appears unnerved by the officer, a person of color, and whips out her phone to record him; soon, she’s threatening violence and is arrested. Then, we see Madison’s Haugen in her apartment watching the video the woman posted to her Facebook page, “Voice of Reason,” with the caption “Watch me own DEI cops.” Haugen reveals later that the woman was a friend she met in spin class, radicalized by conspiracy theories on Facebook after the progressive candidate she campaigned for lost. The scene and details about the friend appear to be fictionalized, but are based on a true part of Haugen’s story. Haugen told The Journal that she took the role on Facebook’s civic integrity team after seeing a family friend radicalized online. “It’s one thing to study misinformation, it’s another to lose someone to it,” she said. Facebook’s algorithm recommended extremist groups In the movie, one of the first major revelations Haugen shares with White’s Horwitz is that 64 percent of people who joined extremist groups on Facebook were sent there by its algorithm. That statistic — in the movie and real life — became the basis of a May 2020 article in The Journal. In the real article, Horwitz and co-author Deepa Seetharaman wrote that a 2016 internal Facebook presentation found “64% of all extremist group joins are due to our recommendation tools.” It added, “Our recommendation systems grow the problem.” At the time of the 2020 article’s publication, a Facebook spokesperson told The Journal it had since strengthened protections and “are not the same company today.” A shift in Facebook’s algorithm promoted rage As they hunt through pages of documents in the movie, Haugen and Horwitz keep trying to figure out why Facebook tuned its recommendation algorithm to reward “Meaningful Social Interactions” (MSI), rather than likes, in 2018. Haugen senses favoring MSI could be driving users like her friend toward radicalization, but she and Horwitz initially aren’t sure how — especially since Facebook publicly said the shift was expected to undercut engagement. They come to understand that the new ranking system weighted emoji reactions and reshares much more highly than likes; Zuckerberg and other executives knew this change would promote rage-sharing. That’s a fairly accurate translation of what we know about MSI. Zuckerberg promoted the shift as a way to correct for a trend of “public content” from brands and media “crowding out the personal moments that lead us to connect more with each other.” Though he anticipated the change would be good for users, he said it would actually hurt Facebook’s engagement. But, he said, “if we do the right thing, I believe that will be good for our community and our business over the long term too.” In an installment of The Journal’s “Facebook Files” series in 2021, however, Horwitz and co-author Keach Hagey found that Facebook employees had warned that prioritizing MSI was promoting angrier engagement. Documents obtained by The Journal showed that leading up to the change, Facebook had been concerned about declining engagement from users through actions like resharing or commenting. To combat this, the documents showed, Facebook tried to encourage more original posts and resharing. While Facebook found some positive user benefits of the change, researchers found, “Misinformation, toxicity, and violent content are inordinately prevalent among reshares.” Zuckerberg, in the movie and apparently real life, resisted some mitigation proposals that would damage engagement. Meta has downplayed the significance of MSI. In a statement to The Journal at the time, Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said, “Is a ranking change the source of the world’s divisions? No.” Instagram made teen girls feel worse about their bodies In the movie, Haugen’s colleague shares a thumb drive with documents including a study about how Instagram harms teen girls’ body image. She tells Haugen to get the word out before the company starts marketing Instagram Kids. It’s not clear if this colleague actually existed, but the information she shares appears to be based on an internal study that found 32 percent of teen girls surveyed who said they felt bad about their bodies felt worse after using Instagram. Instagram had indeed planned to launch a service specifically for kids under 13, but announced shortly amid the uproar from the “Facebook Files” release that it was pausing the project to work through concerns. An early Facebook investor encouraged Zuckerberg to change As Strong’s Zuckerberg preps for the 2021 congressional hearing in the film, sitting on a stage behind a desk and rehearsing answers with his team, a venture capitalist named Charlie emerges from the shadows. Charlie, played by comedian Bill Burr, gives Zuckerberg feedback and urges him to moderate political ads. Movie-Zuckerberg says he’s upset with Charlie after he wrote a scathing op-ed, and reminds him he 100x’d his investment, which would have been worth over $1 billion if he’d held his position. Charlie is inspired by real-life Facebook investor-turned-critic Roger McNamee, an executive producer of the film. McNamee published an op-ed in The Guardian in 2017 charging that Facebook and Google “threaten public health – and democracy,” and in 2019 published the book Zucked: Waking Up to the Facebook Catastrophe. Sorkin told Vanity Fair that although McNamee was game to be depicted in the movie, “it was made clear” that “there might be a problem with Facebook” in depicting the conversation between the VC character and Zuckerberg in the movie. So the character became a fictionalized version inspired by McNamee, instead. Facebook’s civic integrity team was “absorbed” In the film, Haugen seems dejected when she realizes that the civic integrity team she works on — which worked on worldwide election-related risks including misinformation — will likely be dissolved, and she’ll be reassigned. A Facebook executive assures the team that even if that were to happen, the work would be “absorbed” into other teams, and it would only be beneficial to their work. This reflects how the company communicated the change in structure following the 2020 US election. In her “60 Minutes” interview in 2021, Haugen said, “when they got rid of Civic Integrity, it was the moment where I was like, ‘I don’t trust that they’re willing to actually invest what needs to be invested to keep Facebook from being dangerous.’” (That’s actually when Haugen first responded to Horwitz’ initial outreach on LinkedIn.) Meta executive Guy Rosen responded at the time that the team was not disbanded, but rather “integrated” into “a larger Central Integrity team so that the incredible work pioneered for elections could be applied even further, for example across health related issues. Their work continues to this day.” Zuckerberg’s office was bulletproofed Haugen’s film character mentions that Zuckerberg has bullet-proof features in his office, which appears to be based in reality. A 2019 report from Business Insider found that a “glass-walled conference room” he would sometimes work from had “bullet-resistant windows and a panic button.” It took time for Haugen and Horwitz to build a strong source-reporter relationship The movie depicts a push-and-pull relationship between Haugen and Horwitz, as the journalist tries to get Haugen to share more information without crossing a delicate ethical line of soliciting her to steal confidential documents. As Haugen decides whether or not to go the extra mile, she also becomes frustrated with Horwitz for not making more progress on his own. The two meet regularly on a hiking path, where Horwitz eventually gives Haugen a burner phone to communicate with him and on which she later takes pictures of internal documents. At one point, Horwitz even travels to Puerto Rico to collect more information from Haugen, after she relocated there during the pandemic. These details all seem to mostly follow the true course of their source building relationship. Haugen told The New York Times in 2021 that she had “auditioned” Horwitz for some time, and decided to give him the scoop because she found him to be “less sensationalistic than other choices I could have made.” Horwitz acknowledged in an on-stage interview with Haugen in 2022 that “things got tense between us” at times, in part because Haugen had concerns about The Journal’s institutional approach, and in part over some messiness about when certain information was released by other publications or agencies Haugen worked with. Haugen really did relocate to Puerto Rico during the pandemic, and Horwitz also visited her to collect information, though the timeline of those travels is different than in the movie. Haugen invited him to Puerto Rico once she realized Facebook’s policies prevented her from working from a US territory, prompting a deadline to quit or move. She chose to quit, meaning the pair had one last period of time they could access internal documents at Facebook. Speaking to Horwitz on stage in 2022, Haugen said she was “so grateful that you put in a huge amount of effort to just be there and make sure that we asked as many questions as we could so history got to have some kind of record for it.”

articles.title: 81 US military aircraft, drones damaged during Iran war: Report
articles.summary: At least 81 U.S. military aircraft and drones have been damaged or destroyed since the war against Iran began early this year, according to a new report prepared for members of Congress. The Monday report, produced by the Congressional Research Service (CRS), showed the military has sustained losses of uncrewed platforms, including 45 MQ-9 Reaper…
articles.body:
At least 81 U.S. military aircraft and drones have been damaged or destroyed since the war against Iran began early this year, according to a new report prepared for members of Congress.

The Monday report, produced by the Congressional Research Service (CRS), showed the military has sustained losses of uncrewed platforms, including 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones, three MQ-1 Predator drones and one MQ-4C Triton long-endurance aircraft.

The U.S. fighter jet fleet took a beating. Twelve F-15E Strike Eagle fighters were damaged since the war began Feb. 28, including three destroyed in Kuwait by friendly fire and eight that sustained damage in an Iranian military attack in Jordan.

One A-10 Thunderbolt II ground-attack aircraft was destroyed by Iran, while another was damaged in Jordan, according to the four-page report. One F-35A Lightning II fighter aircraft was also damaged.

The U.S. Central Command (Centcom), which oversees the U.S. forces in the Middle East, declined to comment on the report.

Seven KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refueling aircraft have been affected by the war, with one crashing in Iraq that resulted in the deaths of all six aircrew members. The second one made an emergency landing. Five KC-135 Stratotankers were damaged in Saudi Arabia.

One E-3 Sentry airborne early warning-and-control system aircraft was damaged at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, while two MC-130J Commando II special operations aircraft were intentionally destroyed in April while supporting search-and-rescue operations for a downed F-15E, according to the report.

The CRS report comes as the cost of the war has gone up. Centcom told congressional defense committees in mid-September that the price tag of the conflict was $43.6 billion. The Pentagon’s estimate did not include the $1.5 billion for fuel and other costs.

A report from the Congressional Budget Office warned the war could drive up inflation early next year.

President Trump and other administration officials have defended the reasons for launching the war. The commander in chief said recently it is possible the conflict could cost the Republican Party the majority in Congress.

A Pentagon watchdog’s report from last month said U.S. diplomatic facilities in four Persian Gulf countries — Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — sustained $184 million in estimated damage from Iranian military strikes.

images.caption: A U.S. MQ-9 drone is on display during an air show at Kandahar Airfield, Afghanistan, Jan. 23, 2018.

articles.title: Trump’s tariffs were meant to shrink the trade deficit—but the $106 billion gap just reached its widest since before ‘Liberation Day’
articles.summary: The Trump administration has called the trade deficit a “national emergency,” but economists say it’s actually a sign of a resilient American economy.
articles.body:
During President Donald Trump's announcement of "Liberation Day" in April 2025, which would bring with it a raft of aggressive tariffs, Trump claimed the import taxes would slash the U.S.'s stubborn trade deficit , or when a country buys more goods from overseas than it sells.

"They're a national emergency that threatens our security and our very way of life," he said at the time. "It's a very great threat to our country."

But 17 months later, the administration's import taxes haven't closed that deficit at all. In fact, the trade deficit is now the largest it's been since Trump implemented tariffs, and economists are pouring cold water on the very idea that a widening trade gap is even a threat.

The trade deficit grew by 13.7% to $105.6 billion from July to August, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis, the highest it's been since March 2025's $140 billion . While imports increased by 4.3% to $420.8 billion, exports increased, but at a slower rate, growing 2.2% to $205.7 billion.

Experts suggest the growing deficit is largely a result of the AI boom, which has created a mass demand in the U.S. for overseas hardware, spiking imports. AI demand single-handedly added $200 billion to the U.S. trade deficit in April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis.

"The U.S. economy does a bunch of stuff that other countries can't do; one of them is … this AI boom," Tarek Hassan, a professor of economics at Boston University, told Fortune . "And because of the AI boom, foreigners still want to invest in the United States, which is a good thing."

Tariffs have been the cornerstone of Trump's second administration, and the president has justified the levies with promises of more U.S. manufacturing jobs, as well as a cash windfall to be redistributed to the American people—neither of which has come to fruition.

To Trump, the trade deficit was representative of other countries taking advantage of the U.S., or of America's wealth leaving the country, and protectionist measures were the only way to restore U.S. trade dominance.

"Capital goods imports remain at a record high, more evidence that the President Trump's economic policies have led to a manufacturing renaissance." White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Fortune in a statement. "The president's push to reindustrialize the United States continues to pay off as trillions of dollars in manufacturing investments materialize."

But economists see things differently. They argue Trump's whipsaw tariff approach that was meant to slash the deficit was actually, in part, responsible for its widening. They also say they believe Trump's insistence on the gap being a negative economic indicator is actually ignoring evidence of a resilient U.S. economy.

images.caption: The U.S. trade deficit is now at its highest since President Donald Trump introduced sweeping tariffs on “Liberation Day” in April 2025. · Fortune · Chip Somodevilla—Getty Images

articles.title: It appears .agent and .agi are about to be the hot new domains
articles.summary: The ICANN applications for new top-level domains include everything from .openai to .jackpot.
articles.body: For the first time in years, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers — better known as ICANN — is accepting applications for new top-level domains. These are the suffixes at the end of all URLs, and you may know them as things like .com, .org, and .pizza. ICANN just announced the 1,615 applications that have been submitted so far, from 481 different applicants. The trend will not surprise you: AI is everywhere. Ten different companies, including both Meta and OpenAI, applied for the .agent domain. Seven, including OpenAI, applied for .agi. Six, including OpenAI, applied for .asi, clearly attempting to get in on President Trump’s demand to switch from “artificial intelligence” to “super intelligence.” Four companies applied for .intelligence, and Meta is one of two interested in the preposterously long .superintelligence. (OpenAI applied for a total of 15 TLDs; Meta wants a whopping 21.) There are, broadly, two types of domains in these applications. One is more generic, the kind of thing lots of people or companies might use. There are hundreds of those in this current batch, from .geek to .haha to .anime to .jackpot. There’s also my personal favorite new one, .itiswhatitis. The other is purely branded, giving a company its own TLD to use for its own purposes. There are 345 brand applications in this batch, including everything from .applebees and .bankofamerica to .zillow and .zoom. Meta applied for .facebook, .instagram, .messenger, .meta, .frommeta, and .threads, which it could use for many purposes; Bluesky applied for .bsky with the apparent intention of weaving the domain into its usernames; OpenAI applied for .chatgpt, .codex, .openai, .gpt, and others; Anthropic wants .anthropic and .claude. These strings could ultimately make for memorable product pages, social media usernames, and much more besides. It has mostly been a tough road for these alternate TLDs over the last few years. Some, like .ai or .app, have become somewhat popular thanks to various tech trends, but most people just never got used to the idea of typing .restaurant or .babysitting, and .com and a few others have actually become more important than ever. It’s interesting to see so many brands go for their own domain, which only Google and a few others have accomplished before. This is but one step in the process of creating a new top-level domain, and nothing will be made official before sometime next year. But it appears that even as the world becomes more filled with and mediated by AI, great domain names continue to matter. Even the AI companies think so.

articles.title: The Fed was unanimous about raising rates in September. Economic signals have since changed.
articles.summary: The Fed voted unanimously on Sept. 16 to raise rates, the first hike in three years.
articles.body:
Minutes from the Federal Reserve's September policy meeting reflect unanimous agreement among officials that interest rates needed to be higher to combat persistent inflation.

"Participants generally emphasized that inflation remained elevated while the labor market appeared to be near full employment, with some signs of strengthening, and that economic activity was expanding at a solid pace. Furthermore, almost all participants assessed that, while inflation risks were tilted to the upside, risks to the labor market had diminished and were now broadly balanced," minutes from the Sept. 16 meeting released Wednesday stated.

"Based on the outlook and the changing balance of risks, all participants viewed a higher target range for the federal funds rate as appropriate."

The Fed voted unanimously on Sept. 16 to raise rates, the first hike in three years . And at the time, most Federal Open Market Committee members saw a need for at least one more 25 basis point rate hike this year.

Markets were banking on a hike and expecting more to come.

But economic data released in the past few weeks has changed the picture considerably. "Core" PCE, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, rose a relatively cool 3% in August , beating expectations for a rise of 3.3% and marking a drop from 3.3% in July. Meanwhile, September jobs numbers fell far short of economists' expectations, with a gain of just 29,000 jobs , while the unemployment rate edged up to 4.2% from 4.1%.

That less rosy jobs picture, combined with a more positive read on inflation, had analysts — and some Fed officials — throwing cold water on the notion of another rate hike this month.

"This data won't shift the broader decision-making calculus for the Fed as inflation remains the supreme concern," Chris Hodge, chief economist for Natixis, previously told Yahoo Finance. "But with wages lower and the jobs picture a bit less rosy, it certainly decreases the urgency to hike in October (and perhaps December if inflation data cooperates)."

Even before the September job report, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed president John Williams had already begun to temper expectations for a rate hike later this month . Both struck a more cautious tone than several of their colleagues, acknowledging that inflation has remained too high, but that the central bank should take time to assess whether it's on a downward path.

Williams said that, after raising rates in September, he sees "no need for urgency" and that "we have time to gather more information."

articles.title: Robert Rubin Warns AI Boom Carries Risks for US Economy, Markets
articles.summary: Former Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin warned that the artificial-intelligence investment boom could bring major productivity gains but also create financial...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Former Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin warned that the artificial-intelligence investment boom could bring major productivity gains but also create financial and social risks that markets may not be fully pricing.

Rubin, who served as Treasury chief during the internet boom in the late 1990s, said he's particularly concerned about "circularity risk" in the AI ecosystem. The term refers to the overlapping of commitments among suppliers, customers and investors — such as between chipmakers and software firms.

"Some of these very big AI companies have enormous commitments, and then there are a lot of suppliers, and a lot of suppliers have borrowed against those commitments," Rubin said in an interview at the Greenwich Economic Forum Tuesday. "What happens if they can't fulfill those commitments or all those borrowed against them? It's called circularity risk."

The risk of some disruption — where one party breaks its commitments, causing cascading failures — is meaningful, according to Rubin. The former Goldman Sachs co-chairman described it as not "near zero."

The scale of debt issuance this year by firms building data centers and developing AI software has been such that many market participants say it's contributed to an increase in borrowing costs globally. Benchmark government bond yields have climbed further this week, with 10-year Treasury rates hitting their highest level since 2002.

That's in turn propelling government debt servicing costs, stoking concerns about fiscal sustainability in the US, France and elsewhere. Rubin, who joined President Bill Clinton's administration at a time when worries over budget deficits were widely shared, said angst over the scale of borrowing is beginning to be evident.

"I think what's happening right now is some realization about our fiscal situation beginning to affect markets in a way it hasn't for a long time," he said.

He also pointed to inflation and a broader loss of confidence in the government's ability to address fiscal problems. "When you have adverse or unstable fiscal conditions, it can affect confidence more broadly in the ability of your government to deal with this problem," he said.

images.caption: Former Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin · Bloomberg · Bloomberg

articles.title: Lawmakers demand answers on Amateur Athletic Union sex abuse scandal
articles.summary: A bipartisan group of lawmakers is looking for answers from the Amateur Athletic Union (AAU) over its handling of sex abuse allegations within its ranks. In a letter to AAU leadership, House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) and ranking member Frank Pallone Jr. (D-N.J.) called it “unacceptable that AAU is failing to…
articles.body:
A bipartisan group of lawmakers is looking for answers from the Amateur Athletic Union (AAU) over its handling of sex abuse allegations within its ranks.

In a letter to AAU leadership, House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) and ranking member Frank Pallone Jr. (D-N.J.) called it “unacceptable that AAU is failing to implement standard reforms to protect child athletes, and is misleading the public, parents, and athletes about preventative measures in place within AAU sports.”

The letter comes after the publication of an investigation from ProPublica in August that found the AAU has not put in place promised reforms around sex abuse by coaches and other officials following a 2011 scandal.

After the AAU said it would keep coaches banned for misconduct by other youth sports groups out of its ranks, ProPublica found eight banned coaches working with kids in the AAU.

“ProPublica’s reporting describes numerous abuse cases involving AAU coaches that occurred even after the organization’s updated child protection policies were reportedly put in place in 2012,” the lawmakers wrote.

They noted sexual abuse in the Olympic and Paralympic movements led to sweeping reforms implemented by Congress, including the creation of a publicly searchable database of suspended or banned individuals.

“While progress has been made in the Olympic and Paralympic movement, unfortunately we are seeing parallels between what the Committee saw in its prior investigation with what is being uncovered within the AAU today,” the lawmakers wrote.

AAU, in a response to ProPublica when its investigation was published, said it was “committed to protecting its athletes through comprehensive protection policies overseen by our Compliance Department.”

The organization insisted protecting young athletes “is at the forefront of our safety measures such as a verified identity check and mandatory background screenings for all non-athlete AAU members, including coaches.”

The AAU today has almost 800,000 athletes competing in more than 50 sports across the U.S., including basketball, soccer and volleyball.

articles.title: Cantwell unveils new AI framework
articles.summary: Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee, unveiled a framework Wednesday for regulating artificial intelligence amid growing pressure on lawmakers to address the technology’s risks. Cantwell laid out a set of principles for how Congress and the executive branch should approach AI, arguing that to “manage risks…
articles.body:
Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee, unveiled a framework Wednesday for regulating artificial intelligence amid growing pressure on lawmakers to address the technology’s risks.

Cantwell laid out a set of principles for how Congress and the executive branch should approach AI, arguing that to “manage risks from advanced AI systems we need clear safety standards, continuous testing, and reporting of serious failures.”

“America can lead the world in AI by building systems that are not only more capable, but safer and more secure,” she added in a statement.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

She suggested the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) should be in charge of developing standards to protect against catastrophic harms from AI models, such as AI-enabled cyberattacks, biological and chemical threats or loss of human control.

This has become top of mind for lawmakers, after several AI researchers warned last month that the technology could have dire consequences for humanity. A series of incidents in which AI agents hacked into other companies or acted in unexpected ways has further fueled concerns .

Cantwell also argued that government and independent experts should continually scrutinize and stress test models and that AI firms should be subject to comprehensive audits by independent firms.

Under her framework, developers would be responsible for disclosing safety and security risks and incidents and remain liable for unlawful conduct or harm caused by their AI models.

She also called for the government to work with companies on defensive AI capabilities and urged the U.S. to take on a leadership role in creating common global standards on the technology.

Cantwell could play a crucial role in developing AI rules next year if Democrats take the Senate in the upcoming midterms and she becomes chair of the Senate Commerce Committee, which has jurisdiction over key tech policy issues.

articles.title: An AI-generated Rumpelstiltskin meme is freaking out much of the internet
articles.summary: Rumpelstiltskin famously spun straw into gold.
articles.body: Rumpelstiltskin famously spun straw into gold. Now, AI has spun the fairy-tale character into an eerie internet meme. In recent days, a clip began circulating widely online featuring what many described as a “creepy” imp-like character. The imp approaches a woman sitting in a heap of straw and dances before her while she’s frightened to tears. Then, he turns all the straw in the room into gold coins, causing her to exclaim with joy. She kisses him, turning him into a prince. It’s a scene reminiscent of the German fairy tale about Rumpelstiltskin, a magical imp who spins straw into gold for a poor miller’s daughter. The bizarre clip, which looks straight out of an old movie, sent people searching for the film it must have originated from. Some were convinced it was part of the 1987 “Rumpelstiltskin” film, a musical adaptation of the classic tale. It took days before viewers began realizing it was simply AI-generated. By then, the meme had already become a viral format, and users cared little about its AI origins. The original clip was posted online in August by self-described AI artist and filmmaker Tatyana Tereshchenko. Over the past week, users began setting the clip to the rapper Riff Raff’s song “Tip Toe Wing In My Jawwdinz,” turning it into a full-fledged meme. One of the first users to popularize it, according to the online meme database Know Your Meme, paired the clip with the caption: “The type of dreams I be having after taking dollar store melatonin.” It racked up more than 900,000 views on TikTok in less than a week. Others used the clip to describe scenarios like “creeping downstairs at 2am for a lil treat,” “having to walk the aisle in Payless shoe to make sure our $15 shoes fit just right,” and “acing the field sobriety test” at a traffic stop. Internet users quickly found themselves obsessed with the meme. As one user put it: “It’s Stuck in my head all day. That little guy is so creepy.” AI-generated media has increasingly infiltrated mainstream internet culture by gaining organic traction, whether people realize the base material was AI-generated or not. In 2023, an AI-generated image of Pope Francis in a trendy puffer jacket fooled the internet, becoming the first viral meme to emerge from AI material. And in 2024, outlandish AI-generated images — of Jesus made of shrimp, built with plastic bottles or carved out of sand — spread across Facebook and became another internet meme format, despite the obvious AI component. This kind of content, typically labeled “AI slop,” appears to make for fertile meme fodder. Its obvious artificiality and absurdity fit neatly into an online meme culture that often revels in the uncanny. Similarly, after users realized the Rumpelstiltskin meme was made with AI, the clip quickly became a template for users to insert their own characters. People have since replaced the imp with fictional people like Sam and Dean Winchester and Wednesday Addams, public figures like Gypsy-Rose Blanchard and even mascots like Ronald McDonald. One TikTok account dedicated to reposting variations of the meme has racked up more than 65,000 followers within a few days. Some are even re-enacting the AI-generated clip in real life. Others, however, are already eager for the meme to finish its shelf life on the internet, lamenting that they’re tired of the “scary” little imp.

articles.summary:

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln’s controversial deployment comes to an end
articles.summary: Welcome to The Hill’s Defense & NatSec newsletter {beacon} Defense &National Security Defense &National Security The Big Story USS Abraham Lincoln’s deployment finally comes to an end The USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group has returned to the U.S. after a lengthy deployment that grew controversial after it was rerouted to the Middle East for…
articles.body:
USS Abraham Lincoln’s deployment finally comes to an end

The USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group has returned to the U.S. after a lengthy deployment that grew controversial after it was rerouted to the Middle East for the Iran war.

The crew was met by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth Wednesday in San Diego, where he presented them with the highest unit award, the Presidential Unit Citation .

Hegseth praised the crew for supporting the U.S. military’s operations against Iran and helping enforce the naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, saying the strike group “projected decisive combat power and established maritime advantage to achieve the president’s strategic objectives and strengthen the security” of the United States.

The citation comes after the Lincoln, a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, endured an extended deployment in the U.S. Central Command theater, including spending over 260 consecutive days at sea without a port call, per a Navy record.

But the deployment was bogged down by reports of debilitating conditions aboard the aircraft carrier, including degrading mental health of the crew, poor living conditions and food supply challenges, causing scrutiny among Democratic lawmakers.

Last month the Navy revealed that eight sailors of the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during the extended deployment.

Hegseth on Wednesday sought to downplay the issues , accusing members of the press of attempting to “turn the USS Abraham Lincoln into some sort of a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale, or a symbol of a failed mission.”

He continued: “When I talk to your leadership, and I have had a chance to talk to a number of you, I know it’s the exact opposite .”

Welcome to The Hill’s Defense & National Security newsletter, I’m Ellen Mitchell — your guide to the latest developments at the Pentagon, on Capitol Hill and beyond.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday wrestled with a case about whether the Air Force needs to conduct environmental review before its munitions detonations in Guam.

The execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting, is set for December, according to the U.S. Army.

articles.title: FDA: Mifepristone review won’t be done until March
articles.summary: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) won’t publish its safety review of the abortion drug mifepristone until March, it disclosed in a Wednesday court filing, adding that it won’t impose any new restrictions on the pill before that point. The revelations are likely to further anger anti-abortion activists, who have been losing patience with the…
articles.body:
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) won’t publish its safety review of the abortion drug mifepristone until March, it disclosed in a Wednesday court filing, adding that it won’t impose any new restrictions on the pill before that point.

The revelations are likely to further anger anti-abortion activists, who have been losing patience with the Trump administration over what they say is the slow pace of the FDA’s review and failure to crack down on blue state doctors who send the pills across state lines.

In a five-page update filed in a Louisiana federal court, the agency said it is on track to obtain study results by mid-December but won’t finish its report until March.

The agency confirmed it is separately reviewing the safety program that regulates the distribution and use of mifepristone, called a “Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy” — a protocol the FDA uses for drugs with “serious safety concerns.”

That process could take much longer, as the FDA said it will need to review the hundreds of citations included in various citizen petitions urging changes to the prescribing rules, such as the in-person dispensing requirement.

“Following completion of its study and review, FDA will decide whether changes to the Mifepristone REMS Program are necessary and, if applicable, initiate any such changes in accordance with established processes,” the agency wrote. “FDA anticipates that it will be able to provide an update to its estimated date of completion as more information becomes known, particularly in March 2027 when it expects to complete its report on the final study results.”

Abortion rights groups slammed the review as nothing more than a political stunt and said the administration is deliberately delaying its release until after November’s midterm elections.

“Mifepristone is a safe and effective medication backed by decades of science – this ‘review’ is an unnecessary political stunt,” Reproductive Freedom for All President and CEO Mini Timmaraju said in a statement. “The administration is delaying this report because attacks on medication abortion will backfire with voters, but extremists will try to ban abortion as soon as the election is over.”

FDA’s disclosure Wednesday stems from a lawsuit in Louisiana, one of three the agency is facing regarding mifepristone. The other legal challenges came out of Missouri and Texas.

A federal judge paused the Texas case on Aug. 31, while the Missouri case is still being briefed.

Medication has become the most common method of abortion since the 2022 overturning of Roe v. Wade, with much of that increase coming from telehealth prescriptions.

The Louisiana lawsuit challenges Biden-era FDA rules that allow the drug to be prescribed virtually and mailed to patients.

The case has put the Trump administration in an awkward political bind; it won’t defend the Biden administration’s moves, but it also believes Louisiana doesn’t have standing to sue.

Anti-abortion groups hope the review will result in restrictions on mifepristone, but they want the FDA to move faster.

Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, said in a statement ahead of Wednesday’s update that she wants FDA to include a non-peer-reviewed analysis released last year by the conservative Ethics and Public Policy Center, which critics have called “flawed” and “junk science.”

FDA said it is reviewing data contained within Sentinel, a national database partnered with insurers, hospitals, electronic health records and academic institutions, among other groups.

images.caption: Boxes of the drug mifepristone sit on a shelf at the West Alabama Women’s Center in Tuscaloosa, Ala., March 16, 2022.

articles.title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo 11 on the moon, dies at 90
articles.summary: Pioneering computer scientist led the development of the software for Nasa's Apollo mission and was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
articles.body:
The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90.

Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering".

Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September.

"To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream.

Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division.

It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon.

"I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019.

In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring.

The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved.

But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT.

The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her.

In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel.

At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space".

Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958.

She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree.

From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts.

"We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media.

"Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said.

Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT.

images.caption: Hamilton after she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016

articles.title: Fed's Waller sees additional rate hikes to get inflation down faster
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Chris Waller said in a speech Thursday that he expects the Fed will need to enact more interest rate hikes to bring down inflation f...
articles.body:
Federal Reserve Governor Chris Waller said in a speech Thursday that he expects the Fed will need to enact more interest rate hikes to bring down inflation faster if economic data comes in as he expects.

"If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2% goal," Waller said at the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye İstanbul Economic Forum. "But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."

Waller noted a convergence of factors have gelled into persistent inflationary forces, including hopes for a quick ending to the Middle East conflict and warnings that low inventories and damaged infrastructure could keep oil prices high through 2027. He also pointed out that the artificial intelligence build-out has significantly driven up high-tech consumer prices , and projections of its size have ballooned. Additionally, he said, continuing trade conflicts threaten new tariffs that could put upward pressure on inflation yet again.

"When the first inflation reading for August came in hot just before the FOMC's September meeting, it was impossible to deny that inflation was still too high and not making sufficient progress toward our target," Waller said.

Waller sees economic activity strengthening in the second half of this year, and says he's "not greatly concerned" that higher interest rates threaten to markedly slow down the economy.

"But I am concerned that the recent acceleration in inflation — after what soon will be five and a half years of it above the FOMC's target — will lead consumers, investors, and price-setting businesses to revise up their expectations for future inflation."

He noted that he sees the economy in roughly the same place as it was at the time of the Fed's policy meeting in mid-September.

"Overall, the new data reinforce my view that the labor market is stable and inflation is too high," he said. "For at least the near term, policy will be focused on the inflation side of our mandate."

Waller also made a point of sharing how he believes the Fed should communicate its interest rate expectations . He doesn't think choosing to say nothing or offering a strong indication of what the Fed will do is how the central bank should communicate. Rather, he believes an in-between approach of signaling the amount of rate hikes over some time interval, while not saying what the pace of hikes will be or how large they will be, would offer flexibility, while keeping the public informed.

articles.title: UK airbase plot expands fears of Iran’s military capabilities
articles.summary: The U.S. military’s abrupt withdrawal of all of its bombers from a British air base in response to a possible terrorist attack has expanded fears over Iran’s ability to strike targets outside the Middle East — and well outside its missile range. The threat, reported to be a potential drone attack ordered by Iran’s Islamic…
articles.body:
The U.S. military’s abrupt withdrawal of all of its bombers from a British air base in response to a possible terrorist attack has expanded fears over Iran’s ability to strike targets outside the Middle East — and well outside its missile range.

The threat, reported to be a potential drone attack ordered by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, prompted Washington on Sunday to relocate the 12 Air Force B-1 bombers stationed at RAF Fairford in southern England back to home stations in the United States.

The incident, which comes amid the Trump administration’s now seven-month war against Iran, has renewed worries about the vulnerability of the West’s military bases and assets.

“It obviously was quite serious if the U.S. felt compelled to so abruptly move the bombers,” Mona Yacoubian, the director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said of the incident.

“Unfortunately, I do think this could be part of a longer-term trend in which we see Iran in various ways relying on these asymmetric drone, in particular, capabilities, taking lessons from other war zones,” she told The Hill.

One of those war zones is Ukraine, where Kyiv has massively expanded its counterattack capabilities through drones. In one coordinated attack dubbed “Operation Spiderweb,” Ukraine smuggled truckloads of drones into Russia to strike five military bases inside the country.

Even as the full details around the alleged U.K. plot remain unknown, the incident has highlighted how modern warfare can threaten areas far from the frontlines, forcing the U.S. to shift people, assets and equipment.

President Trump on Monday told reporters that the U.S. government moved the bombers “around a little bit, not very far” as the British airbase was under threat of attack by Iran.

“There was some threats . . . so why should we leave them there?” Trump said as he departed the White House, referring to the warplanes.

Vice President Vance the same day said the U.S. military moved the bombers “out of an abundance of caution trying to protect our guys,” accusing Tehran in general of plotting attacks against the U.S. and other countries.

“We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are, you know they’re trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engage in acts of terrorism against the United States and against a lot of other people as well,” Vance told reporters at Joint Base Andrews enroute to Alaska.

“We are being extremely cautious,” he added.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, sought to downplay the move, describing it as “not unusual, adding that he “wouldn’t directly tie” the British terror plot to the bomber movements.

However, it would not be the first time the U.S. has been forced to move military assets in Europe over perceived Iranian threats.

In August, two Air Force KC-135 refueling planes were relocated from a Bulgarian air base after Tehran issued a warning to the Balkan nation over allowing their territory to be a jumping-off point for American military action against the regime. Iran said it “has the right to target the point of origin and source of any act of aggression against” it.

Tehran has said that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces.”

Iran also has proven it can strike far outside its borders. An Iranian drone struck a British airbase in Cyprus in March, the same month it fired two ballistic missiles at the remote U.K.-U.S. base in the Indian Ocean known as Diego Garcia.

The regime also killed three U.S. service members with ballistic missile and drone attacks in Jordan in July.

In the latest incident pinned on Iran, British authorities said they had thwarted an alleged terrorist plot, initially arresting five men on explosives and terror charges near RAF Fairford on Sept. 27. The men, all five of whom are British nationals in their 20s, were released on bail a day later, but two additional men were later arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham last week said his government believes that Iran “played a part” in the incident. Iran has denied the accusations.

More recently, U.S. and British officials told The New York Times that the two allies believe Iran plotted to strike aircraft and kill some of the several hundred American personnel stationed at RAF Fairford, which the U.S. has used to position B-52 and B-1 bombers as part of the Trump administration’s war against Iran .

Some of the officials told the outlet that the plot was thought to be loosely modeled after the Ukrainian drone attack launched from semi-trucks last year, which destroyed or damaged at least a dozen Russian aircraft.

Yacoubian said there is new knowledge being gained from different war zones “and we will see asymmetric powers like Iran seek to exploit that learning, exploit those lessons, and translate them in new ways to cause problems for the United States.”

She added that while Iran’s attacks outside the Gulf region are not new, the timing suggests the regime seeks to demonstrate it would rather escalate the conflict than capitulate to the U.S. and economic pressure to end the war, pointing to the recent rhetoric between Washington and Tehran.

Trump in September told the United Nations General Assembly he faces a “big decision” on whether to restart a bombing campaign against Iran or broker a peace deal, adding that he could “annihilate” the regime.

And last week, the president said ramped-up military strikes against Iran were “possible” after the November midterm elections.

Adding to speculations of renewed fighting is Washington’s recent movement of more service members to the Middle East, last week sending thousands more sailors and Marines aboard a third aircraft carrier strike group and an additional Marine expeditionary unit.

Tehran, meanwhile, on Monday warned that any new attack could trigger strikes against American interests “without any restrictions,” no matter if it comes before or after the midterms.

“This kind of growing pressure and rhetoric suggests that a new round of confrontation could be in the offing very soon,” Yacoubian said, adding that it’s certain to create more instances of the U.S. being forced to shift its people and weapons.

This “is going to create all kinds of knock-on challenges that, unfortunately, maybe we’re only starting to just see the beginning of that and what that looks like,” she said.

images.caption: Police guard a road leading to RAF Fairford, a US Airbase, after an incident in Fairford, England , Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Alastair Grant)

articles.title: What strangers can learn from your political donation
articles.summary: Federal Election Commission records can expose your name, address, employer and donation history once contributions exceed the $200 threshold.
articles.body: Search your name in the Federal Election Commission's contribution database or on a campaign finance site such as OpenSecrets.org. If you have given enough to trigger federal disclosure requirements, you may be surprised by how much information can be connected to your donation. Depending on the record, that can include your name, mailing address, employer, occupation, donation amount and the political committee that received your money. This is not a data breach. It is part of federal campaign finance disclosure law. And once information about you is public, it can potentially be combined with personal details found elsewhere online. Here's what your political donation can reveal, how that information can be used and what you can do to reduce the rest of your exposure. Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist. See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com. DEM FUNDRAISING GIANT MAKES DAMNING ADMISSION AS GOP PROBES FOREIGN DONATION ALLEGATIONS What's actually in your political donation record Federal campaigns generally must itemize an individual's contributions once that person's contributions exceed $200 in the aggregate during the applicable election cycle. For PACs and party committees, the reporting period can be based on the calendar year. An itemized federal contribution can include: One contribution may not seem revealing on its own. The privacy concern grows when those details can be connected with information already available through people-search sites, public records and data brokers. Pay particular attention to your employer and occupation. A people-search profile may already include addresses and relatives, while a campaign finance record can add another verified detail about where you work or what you do. Want to see how much of your personal information is already exposed online? Use the free data exposure scanner at CyberGuy.com to check. How public donation information can add to your online profile A campaign finance record alone provides only part of the picture. Other public sources and people-search sites may reveal much more. Sites such as Spokeo, Whitepages and BeenVerified can contain address histories, possible relatives, phone numbers, email addresses and property information. When information from several sources lines up, someone researching you may be able to build a much more detailed profile. Here is how those pieces can connect. Step 1: They can confirm who you are Names are rarely unique. An address, employer or occupation can help distinguish you from another person with the same name. That makes publicly available information useful for confirming that someone has found the right person. Step 2: They can look for your family Once someone has your name and location, people-search services may make it easier to identify possible relatives. Your political donation record does not normally list your family members. However, information found elsewhere can connect your identity with a spouse, adult child, parent or other relative. That can create opportunities for impersonation scams and highly personalized phishing attempts. HOW HURRICANE CHARITY SCAMS TARGET YOU BEFORE STORMS HIT Step 3: Your workplace can make a scam more convincing Knowing where you work gives a scammer another detail that can make an email, text or phone call feel legitimate. A phishing message that mentions your actual employer or professional role can be more convincing than a generic message because it contains information you recognize. That is why limiting the amount of personal information available across the web can reduce what criminals have to work with. Step 4: Be cautious with personalized donation requests Scammers frequently imitate legitimate organizations, charities and fundraising groups. The FTC warns that fraudulent fundraisers may use familiar-sounding names, pressure people to act quickly or falsely claim someone donated before. There is also an important legal protection around federal campaign finance data. Information copied or obtained from FEC reports about individual contributors cannot legally be sold or used to solicit political or charitable contributions or for commercial purposes. Criminals do not always follow the law, of course. Still, you should be suspicious of any unexpected fundraising request that seems unusually familiar with your personal history. What if you donated through ActBlue or WinRed? Using an online fundraising platform does not automatically make a federal contribution private. For earmarked federal contributions exceeding $200, reporting requirements can include the contributor's name, mailing address, employer, occupation, date and amount. State campaign finance rules are different. Disclosure thresholds and the information made public vary by state, so a contribution that is not itemized under federal rules could still be subject to separate state reporting requirements. What data removal services can and cannot remove This is an important limitation to understand. A data removal service generally cannot erase legally required government records such as federal campaign finance filings. That means an FEC filing is not something a removal service can simply delete. What these services can address is the personal information surrounding that public record. Your campaign finance record might identify your name, mailing address, employer and occupation. Meanwhile, data brokers may have phone numbers, email addresses, relatives, previous addresses and other personal information. Removing those additional profiles can make it harder for someone to connect separate pieces of information about you into one detailed profile. Some data removal services automatically send opt-out requests to data brokers and continue checking for information that may reappear. Others also offer custom removal requests for websites where your personal information is exposed. However, legal and technical restrictions still apply, especially when the information comes from government records or other sources that are required to remain public. You can also submit removal requests yourself. The process takes more time, but reducing the amount of personal information spread across people-search sites and data brokers can make it harder for strangers or scammers to build a detailed profile about you. PAC and party committee reporting rules can use a calendar-year threshold instead. Also remember that some committees voluntarily disclose contributions below the amount they are required to itemize. Check your state records separately State disclosure laws vary significantly. Your state may use a different reporting threshold or disclose different information than the federal system, so check the campaign finance database maintained by your state election authority. Be skeptical of personalized fundraising messages Do not assume a message is legitimate because it mentions a candidate, organization or contribution you recognize. Instead of clicking a link in an unexpected email or text, visit the organization's official website independently. Also be wary of anyone pressuring you to donate immediately or asking you to pay through gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency.
